identification.summary: Shamoon (also called Disttrack) is a destructive disk-wiping malware family used in attacks on Middle Eastern energy and government organizations in 2012, 2016-2017 and 2018. 'Shamoon Group' is a label for whoever operated it, not a single confirmed actor; the 2012 claim came from a persona calling itself Cutting Sword of Justice [S1][S2][S3][S4][S6].
identification.firstObserved: 2012-08: Saudi Aramco reported the attack on 15 August 2012 [S1][S2].
identification.notes: Vendor reporting ties different Shamoon waves to different Iran-linked clusters (Greenbug and Magic Hound credential theft in 2016; APT33 or a group impersonating it in 2018) [S5][S7]. Microsoft tracks APT33/Elfin as Peach Sandstorm (formerly Holmium) [S9]. No source gathered gives a Microsoft name for Shamoon itself, so this record should not be merged with Peach Sandstorm. StoneDrill (Kaspersky) is a separate wiper family with similar style, and its actor link is unresolved [S8].

attribution.confidence: Attribution to Iran is a vendor and press assessment, not a confirmed government finding in the sources gathered. McAfee said APT33, or a group impersonating APT33, was likely behind Shamoon 3 [S7]. Unit 42 said it had no information on attackers or motives beyond links to the 2012 attacks [S4]. Anomali noted the sample was not confirmed as Iranian [S6].
attribution.basis: Self-claim by Cutting Sword of Justice on Pastebin, 15 August 2012 [S2]. Code similarity between the 2012 and 2016-2017 samples [S3][S4]. McAfee comparison of Shamoon 3 tools and domains with FireEye's APT33 reporting [S7]. Symantec suggested stolen credentials may have come from Greenbug, without solid evidence of a link [S5].

objectives: Destruction and disruption of targeted networks. The 2012 claimant framed the attack as opposition to the Al Saud regime [S2]. Aramco said production systems were isolated and unaffected [S1][S2].

targeting.notes: 2012: Saudi Aramco, about 30,000 workstations affected per Aramco [S1][S2]. 2016: Saudi organizations including the General Authority of Civil Aviation [S3][S4]. 2018: oil, gas, energy, telecom and government targets in the Middle East and southern Europe, often via suppliers [S6][S7][S10].

capabilities.summary: Shamoon overwrote data and destroyed master boot records so machines could not boot [S2]. Kaspersky found a hardcoded trigger time of 15 August 2012 08:08 UTC in the 2012 sample [S2]. Shamoon 2 samples carried a non-operational C2 and a fixed wipe time of 2016-11-17 20:45; Unit 42 saw legitimate tools and batch scripts used to push Disttrack to known hostnames [S4]. Shamoon 3 used a .NET wiper with an unobfuscated toolkit and embedded ASCII art with a Quran verse that is never shown to victims [S6]. Palo Alto reported it overwrote the MBR, partitions and files with random data [S10].

campaigns.name: Saudi Aramco wiper attack
campaigns.summary: Malware hit about 30,000 Aramco workstations on 15 August 2012; the Cutting Sword of Justice claimed it on Pastebin. Employees returned to work 25 August. Production was reported unaffected.

campaigns.name: Shamoon 2 (Saudi organizations)
campaigns.summary: Disttrack variants set to wipe on 17 November and 29 November 2016 hit Saudi organizations including the civil aviation authority. Symantec suggested Greenbug credential theft may have enabled access.

campaigns.name: StoneDrill (related family)
campaigns.summary: Kaspersky found a separate wiper with similar authoring style in Saudi Arabia and one European petrochemical organization; no actor was named.

campaigns.name: Shamoon 3
campaigns.summary: New variant hit Middle East energy, telecom and government targets and Italian contractor Saipem. McAfee assessed APT33 or an impersonator as likely responsible.

diamond.adversary: Unresolved. Claimed by Cutting Sword of Justice in 2012; vendors associate later waves with Iran-linked clusters (Greenbug, Magic Hound, APT33) with caveats [S2][S5][S7].
diamond.capability: Disttrack/Shamoon wiper with scheduled trigger, MBR destruction and scripted network distribution [S2][S4][S6].
diamond.infrastructure: Not established in sources gathered. Shamoon 2 samples used a non-operational C2 address [S4].
diamond.victim: Saudi and Gulf energy, aviation, telecom and government organizations, plus European suppliers and contractors [S1][S3][S6][S10].
diamond.socioPolitical: Claimed motive was opposition to the Saudi monarchy [S2]; Iran-linked attribution rests on vendor assessments and Iran has denied involvement per press summaries [S7].
diamond.technology: Windows domain networks with shared admin credentials and flat reachability from IT to workstations; Aramco's isolated production network limited the impact [S1][S4].

gaps: No government attribution statement was reviewed; CISA AA22-055A and other government pages could not be opened and are not relied on.
WebFetch could not reach securelist.com or cfr.org, so Kaspersky, Unit 42 and CFR primary text was not read. Facts rely on search summaries and press coverage of those reports.
Microsoft naming for Shamoon operators was not found.
Relationship among Cutting Sword of Justice, Greenbug, Magic Hound/APT35, APT33 and OilRig operators is unresolved; do not merge vendor clusters.
Source dates for some secondary articles were taken from URL and snippet context, not confirmed on page.
Whether StoneDrill shares an operator with Shamoon is unresolved.

implications.jipoe: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. STEP 1: Domain controllers, workstation fleets and IT-to-OT boundaries at energy and aviation organizations are key terrain; Aramco's isolated production network limited damage [S1]. STEP 2: Attackers prepare in advance and set timed triggers, often timed near holidays or weekends, so wipe time may be fixed days ahead [S2][S4]. STEP 3: Credential theft, then scripted mass deployment with legitimate tools, then wiper at a preset time [S4][S5]. STEP 4: MLCOA is further destructive attacks on Gulf energy and government networks and their supplier chain [S6][S10]. MDCOA is a wiper wave against coalition-hosting or contractor networks during a regional crisis. Candidate indicators: new admin account use or batch-script distribution, unexpected raw disk driver loads, and scheduled-task or service creation across many hosts shortly before a fixed date [S4].
implications.jcc2: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. (1) Situational awareness: track vendor reports of new Disttrack variants and wipe-date configurations. (2) Authorities: attribution is vendor-level only, so response and sharing should proceed on indicators rather than waiting for attribution [S7]. (3) Mission assurance: maintain offline backups and rebuild capacity, and keep operational networks isolated from enterprise IT as Aramco did [S1]. (4) Coordination: share indicators with Gulf partners and supplier contractors, since 2018 targeting ran through European suppliers [S6][S10].

provenance.importedSummary: Shamoon Group is an Iran-linked threat actor associated with destructive Shamoon wiper operations targeting organizations in the Middle East, especially in the energy sector.
